bullet_groups.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold

feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: The chain of qualifiers ('for a production ... classifier that rates ... by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift') leaves the subject of 'trigger' unclear: is it the classifier or the check? 'grades shift' doesn't say shift relative to what.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a solid drift-detection design on a production system, which backend and MLOps interviewers like. But a reader has to reread it to see that the candidate's code is the scheduled monitor deciding when retraining runs.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: grades shift relative to what (the judge's grades, a baseline window?)
feedback.suggested_direction: Split the bullet into what the check does and what it decides: 'Built a scheduled (EventBridge) LLM-as-judge check on a production Bedrock document classifier that triggers fine-tuning only when its grades drift past a threshold from <baseline>'.

feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: Three stacked service/technique names ('EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check', 'production Amazon Bedrock classifier') come before the reader knows what the check does, and 'its grades' is ambiguous: it could refer to the judge or the classifier.
feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter can't restate this to a hiring manager, so the one production-ML-ops bullet in the role gets skipped.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whose grades shift (the classifier's vs. the judge's), and what problem this saves (e.g. needless retraining)
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the plain purpose (a scheduled check that decides when the document classifier needs retraining), then the method (a second model grading its output), and move 'EventBridge' to Skills or the end.

feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: Two stacked noun phrases ('EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check', 'production Amazon Bedrock classifier') that nobody says out loud. The tail is also ambiguous: 'to trigger fine-tuning' could attach to the classifier ('rates documents ... to trigger fine-tuning') or to the check, and 'its grades' could be the judge's or the classifier's.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader has to re-read to work out which model judges which and what crosses the threshold. That is exactly the mechanism an interviewer will probe, and the bullet blurs it.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whose grades are compared against the threshold (the judge's scores of the classifier, or drift in the classifier's own outputs), and what the scheduled check compares them to
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the plain job in verb form, then the trigger, then the scheduler. Move 'EventBridge' to the end or to Skills. Example shape: 'Built a scheduled check that has an LLM grade our Bedrock document-ranking model and kicks off fine-tuning only when its grades drift past a threshold'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
feedback.problem: The middle of the bullet stacks five technologies ('React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation'). '90% ... preferred' doesn't say what they preferred it over.
feedback.why_it_matters: A backend reader skims past a frontend tech list, and the result is the only number in the bullet. If the comparison isn't stated, the reader can't tell how strong the 90% is.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: preferred over the legacy tool (presumably)
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep React Flow, since it explains the visual editor, and leave the rest of the stack to Skills. State the comparison, e.g. '...which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred over the legacy tool'.

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
feedback.problem: Five technology names in one clause ('React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation') make it read like a stack list rather than a person describing what they built.
feedback.why_it_matters: It dilutes an otherwise strong, easy-to-repeat result (90% preferred) and pushes it to the very end of a full two-line bullet.
feedback.suggested_direction: Cut 'React and TypeScript' or 'Jest-tested' to Skills; keep 'Electron app' and 'visual editor' since they explain what changed for users.

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
feedback.problem: Five technologies packed into the middle (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow, Jest) read as a parenthetical tech dump without the parentheses. 'to make editing smoother' is vague, and 'preferred' doesn't say over what. 'legacy test-data workflow tool' is a noun stack.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader loses what was actually wrong with the old tool and what the rebuild changed. The 90% reads as a satisfaction poll with no stated comparison.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: preferred over the legacy tool (presumably); what was painful about editing before
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep at most 'Electron app with a visual React Flow editor' and move React/TypeScript/Jest to Skills. Say 'preferred it over the old tool'. Replace 'smoother' with the concrete change (e.g. visual editing instead of hand-edited files, if that's the case).

bullet_groups.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
feedback.problem: For a backend reader this is the least relevant bullet, and it has no outcome. It ends at intent ('to help ... pick grasps'), and 'aimed at ICLR' is a submission target, not a result.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a minor cost. It takes two lines of prime space under Experience, and a general SWE reader won't weigh it.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the overlay approach measurably changed grasp selection, if known
feedback.suggested_direction: Leave it as is if no result exists. If a result does exist, state it. Don't add backend framing that isn't true.

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
feedback.problem: Long, single-sentence chain ('...aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps ... in Open3D to help a vision-language model...'); AnyGrasp and Open3D are opaque tool names mid-sentence.
feedback.why_it_matters: The interesting idea (helping a robot pick grips that don't hit the table) is the last thing read; recruiters skip it, as I did on the skim.
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the goal (helping a robot's vision-language model choose grips that avoid collisions), then the method; consider moving 'Open3D' to Skills.

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
feedback.problem: One long chain of relative clauses ('for a project aimed at ICLR that overlays ... to help ... that avoid'). 'that overlays' grammatically attaches to the project or to ICLR, not to the pipeline. 'aimed at ICLR' is a venue name-drop with unclear status (submitted? planned?), and an interviewer will ask. There is no outcome.
feedback.why_it_matters: Reads like a stitched paragraph, not a sentence a person would say. 'aimed at ICLR' invites the credibility question 'was it submitted, and what's your authorship?'
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: submission status and Amar's role on the paper; what 'prompt-tuned' changed
feedback.suggested_direction: Split purpose from venue: put the pipeline's job first (draw candidate grasps onto camera images so a VLM can pick collision-free ones), then 'for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR'. Consider cutting 'in Open3D' to Skills.

bullet_groups.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga’s Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga’s Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
feedback.problem: 'Tortuga’s' is an unexplained product name that comes before the reader knows it's a class scheduler. 'to reduce database load and latency' states intent with no measured change, so the only number (20,000+ visits) describes traffic, not the cache.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a real production backend bullet with real users. But an interviewer can't tell if the cache helped, and will ask about hit rate and invalidation.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: any observed change in DB load or latency after caching, if one exists
feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce the product first ('Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days'), then the cache and what it cached. If there's no measured result, say what was cached (e.g. which queries) and drop the intent clause.

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga’s Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
feedback.problem: 'Tortuga' is never introduced; a reader has to guess it is the class scheduler. 'Prisma ORM queries' adds jargon without explaining the decision.
feedback.why_it_matters: The 20,000+ visits number is a clear user-traction signal but is attached to an unnamed product.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: that Tortuga is the class scheduler
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the product first ('Tortuga, a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits...'), then the caching; 'Prisma ORM' can move to Skills.

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
feedback.problem: The only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the caching work, so it reads as borrowed impact. 'to reduce database load and latency' states an intent with no result. 'Tortuga' is never explained, so the reader has to infer it's the class scheduler.
feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptic sees a team-level traffic metric attached to one person's cache layer and discounts it. An interviewer will ask 'how much did load drop?', and the page has no answer.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether any before/after load or latency measurement exists; that Tortuga is the scheduler's name
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the product once ('Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first month') so the visits are framed as context, not as the cache's result. If no measurement exists, say what the cache keyed on or what it invalidated on instead of an unmeasured 'reduce'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Built the Claude skill’s main search tool by precomputing popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits

feedback.bullet: Built the Claude skill’s main search tool by precomputing popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits
feedback.problem: The stated reason, 'to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits', is the most confusing clause on the page. It's unclear whether the precomputation avoided rate limiting, worked around restricted access, or both. A backend interviewer will also ask straight away how the cached tree stays fresh.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most backend-relevant Capital One bullet: a Postgres-to-Redis precompute layer. The vague reason weakens it, and it raises a question about access controls that the candidate shouldn't have to explain away.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the constraint was query-rate limits on a shared DB, restricted read permissions, or both; what the category tree is keyed on
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint concretely and say what the tree is keyed on, before the technology. For example: '...so the agent queries a cached tree keyed by <category> and doesn’t hit the shared, rate-limited PostgreSQL table on every lookup'.

feedback.bullet: Built the Claude skill’s main search tool by precomputing popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits
feedback.problem: 'Redis-cached category tree' and 'within the database's permission and rate limits' are hard to picture; the bullet doesn't say what the search tool finds or for whom.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader understands it's a search tool but not why limits were the problem, so the engineering decision doesn't land.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the 'permission and rate limits' were blocking (the AI skill querying the table directly?)
feedback.suggested_direction: Say the problem first (the AI skill couldn't query the 270K-row table directly because of access limits), then the fix (precomputed, cached category tree).

feedback.bullet: Built the Claude skill's main search tool by precomputing popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits
feedback.problem: The mechanism is unclear. 'precomputing popular workflows ... into a category tree' doesn't say what the tree is keyed on, and how a cache keeps lookups 'within the database's permission ... limits' isn't obvious. A cache explains rate limits, not permissions. 'Redis-cached category tree' is a noun stack.
feedback.why_it_matters: 'permission limits' is the phrase an interviewer will poke at first. If the answer isn't crisp, it undercuts the strong Capital One bullet above it.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'permission limits' means here (e.g. the skill couldn't query the table directly) and what categories the tree groups workflows by
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint and the design in one sentence without a 'Because ...' preamble, e.g. 'Built ... by precomputing ... so the skill never queried the table directly, keeping it within its access and rate limits'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search

feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search
feedback.problem: 'Claude skill', 'sub-skills' and 'open-ended model search' are terms specific to LLM tooling. A general backend interviewer or recruiter can't picture the before and after.
feedback.why_it_matters: The 65% result is strong, but if the mechanism isn't clear, it reads as prompt tweaking and not as an engineering change (adding deterministic tool calls).
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'workflow generation' produces (the test-data workflows from the previous bullet?)
feedback.suggested_direction: Describe the change in plain terms: the model stopped searching freely and started calling deterministic Python search and validation tools. Tie 'workflow' back to the tool in the bullet above so the reader knows what was generated.

feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search
feedback.problem: 'AI workflow generation' isn't tied back to the test-data tool in bullet one, so the reader isn't sure what is being generated or by whom.
feedback.why_it_matters: A small orientation gap; the 65% number is still memorable.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: that the workflows are the test-data workflows from the tool above
feedback.suggested_direction: Add a short anchor such as 'test-data workflow generation' so the three Capital One bullets read as one story.

feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search
feedback.problem: 'AI workflow generation' doesn't say what a workflow is (it's only explained by the bullet above). 'open-ended model search' is jargon a non-engineer can't restate.
feedback.why_it_matters: Good form and a real mechanism, but a recruiter can't say what got faster.
feedback.suggested_direction: Tie it to the tool above with a few words ('generating test-data workflows with Claude') and replace 'open-ended model search' with 'letting the model search on its own'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end

feedback.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end
feedback.problem: The first two-thirds is C++ container names ('std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map'); the only plain outcome is at the very end, and 'O(1)' is jargon to a non-engineer.
feedback.why_it_matters: The 1.26M events/sec figure is a headline number, but a skimmer has to wade through data-structure syntax to reach it, and a recruiter can't say what the design achieved.
feedback.suggested_direction: Put the goal first (constant-time cancels / fast replay), then the structure in words ('a queue per price level plus a lookup by order ID'); keep 'std::map' only if it explains the choice.

feedback.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end
feedback.problem: 'which ran the full replay' has no sensible antecedent: the design, or the cancels, doesn't run a replay; the engine does. The tacked-on 'which' clause links throughput to the cancel design without showing the two are causally connected. 'std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map' is a dense stack.
feedback.why_it_matters: Structure rule violation (extra clause tacked on). A skeptic reads it as implying O(1) cancels produced 1.26M events/sec, which an HFT-literate interviewer will challenge.
feedback.suggested_direction: Either make throughput the subject ('Replayed the full feed at 1.26M events/sec by ...') or keep the design sentence and drop the dangling 'which'. Spell the structure out in words: 'a FIFO queue per price level, kept in a sorted map, plus a hash map from order ID to its queue position so cancels are O(1)'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff which research topics are popular

feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff which research topics are popular
feedback.problem: 'Co-built' doesn't say which part the candidate owned. 'deployed it to dev' shows the tool only reached a dev environment, and that sits in the middle of the bullet. The infrastructure list ('Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK') reads as a tech list, not a decision.
feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer will ask 'what did you personally build, and is it used?'. As written, the answer could be 'part of a dev-only app'.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part the candidate owned (e.g. the infra/IaC and pipeline vs. the scoring logic)
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the user and the purpose, then the piece the candidate owned (e.g. 'set up the CDK-defined Fargate deployment and GitHub Actions pipeline'). Keep the honest 'dev' scope, but make it a clause and not the headline.

feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff which research topics are popular
feedback.problem: 'Co-built' makes ownership unclear: what did Amar build versus a teammate? The middle is a tech list ('AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK') that reads as keywords rather than a decision. 'deployed it to dev' honestly says it isn't in prod, but it lands as an anticlimax after the deployment stack. 'topic-scoring research tool' is a noun stack.
feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical reader assumes 'co-' means a minor role and reads the three infra names as padding. The bullet never says what Amar engineered.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part Amar owned (scoring logic, infra-as-code, CI pipeline); how a topic's 'popularity' is scored
feedback.suggested_direction: Name Amar's own slice first, keep one infra tool only if it explains a choice, and let Skills carry the rest. Put the audience/purpose before the deployment detail.

bullet_groups.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost

feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
feedback.problem: The phrase 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' parses two ways on first read: 'reserves' can be read as a noun ('Redshift reserves') until the reader reaches 'for patching'. The top bullet on the page, under the strongest brand, needs a second pass.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the first thing a backend screener reads. If they stumble here, the AWS role reads as a vague 'capacity planning' task and not as a real piece of backend work.
feedback.suggested_direction: Put the system and the purpose first and make 'reserve' unambiguously a verb, e.g. 'Writing backtested Java logic that decides how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift should hold back for patching, setting upper and lower bounds to balance availability against cost'.

feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
feedback.problem: 'backtested Java capacity-planning logic' is a noun stack, and 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' is a reduced relative clause that reads at first as 'EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift' as a compound. 'logic' is vague about what Amar owns (a model? a service? a formula?).
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top brand on the page and the first bullet read. A garden-path sentence here costs the skim.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what form the 'logic' takes (a service, a model, a library within an existing service)
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the problem in plain words: Redshift holds spare EC2 capacity for patching; Amar is writing the Java code that decides how much (upper/lower bounds) and backtesting it on history. Add 'that' in 'the EC2 capacity that Redshift reserves'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals

feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' needs a reread: 'real scraped recipes' is the object, but it's easy to read 'GPT-4o mini real' as one phrase. The bullet also stacks three AI terms in a row.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a minor readability cost on an AI bullet that's less central for a backend reader.
feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder to put the purpose first: '...so GPT-4o mini suggests meals grounded in real scraped recipes retrieved with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB'.

feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is a garden-path phrase (double object, reads as 'feed GPT-4o mini' then 'real scraped recipes'). 'RAG meal suggestions' is a noun stack. 'for 93% of meals' is unclear: meals the model suggested, or dining-hall meals?
feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer can't restate it, and an engineer has to re-parse the middle to see that retrieval grounds the model in real recipes.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what a 'meal' is in the 93% (suggested meals rated by testers)
feedback.suggested_direction: Say the purpose in plain words first (suggest meals grounded in real recipes so the model doesn't invent dishes), then the mechanism (SentenceBERT search over scraped recipes), then the 93%. Move ChromaDB to Skills.

bullet_groups.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine's event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine's event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
feedback.problem: Mixes ratio styles ('12.8x the read throughput' vs '22x faster range queries'), and the comparison only reports reads. An LSM tree's main advantage is writes, so a reader wonders whether write results were left out. Why an order-book event log needs either structure isn't stated.
feedback.why_it_matters: A systems interviewer will immediately ask 'and writes?'. A one-sided benchmark looks selected rather than reported.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: write-side result of the comparison, if measured; what reads the event log (replay? queries?)
feedback.suggested_direction: Use one ratio phrasing for both numbers. If write results exist, state the trade-off honestly in place of one of the read numbers; if not, frame it as a read-path comparison.

bullet_groups.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda

feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
feedback.problem: '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (total, per day, per run), so the scale is unanchored. 'S3 staging hops' is jargon.
feedback.why_it_matters: Minor. The bullet is well-formed, but the scale number can't be interpreted.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: 6,000+ per what period
feedback.suggested_direction: Add the period if known; say 'intermediate S3 writes' instead of 'staging hops'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products

feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products
feedback.problem: Pure scale statement with no engineering content; it uses one of three slots in the role.
feedback.why_it_matters: Minor; leadership signal is fine but doesn't support the 'systems engineer' story.
feedback.suggested_direction: Fine to keep; optionally fold into the role header line to free attention for the engineering bullets.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest systems evidence (the C++ order book: 50.9M messages replayed, 99,122/99,123 fills matched, 1.26M events/sec, the B+ tree vs LSM comparison) is last on the page, below the UMIACS robotics bullet and the TerpLabs RAG bullet. The backend and cloud evidence higher up (Postgres to Redis precompute, S3 to Kinesis rewrite, EventBridge drift check) is real but spread out and mixed with LLM and frontend work.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend skimmer gets the AWS, Capital One and Amazon Leo brands at once (good). But the bullets that best prove 'systems-oriented engineer' only reach readers who get to the bottom third. That's where many 7-second screens stop.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Inside each role, order bullets with the backend or data-path bullet first (e.g. at Capital One, put the PostgreSQL/Redis search-tool bullet above the Electron rewrite). Consider whether UMIACS or TerpLabs should come below Projects for backend-targeted versions.

page_feedback.problem: The intended 'systems-oriented engineer' identity rests mostly on the IEX order book project, which sits at the bottom of the page; the experience section reads as cloud + AI tooling.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: On a 7-second skim I took away 'AWS/AI builder', not 'performance-sensitive systems'; the strongest systems evidence is found last.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider whether the order book project's strongest bullet earns a higher position, or whether experience bullets can name the systems aspect (latency, capacity, caching) first.

page_feedback.problem: 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' is an unfamiliar org name next to a famous brand.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter can't tell if this is a student club, a paid contract, or Amazon employment, and might wonder if 'Amazon' is being borrowed.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: clarify in the header what kind of organization this is (e.g. student-run contracting group) and keep the client in parentheses.

page_feedback.problem: Human voice across the page: about half the bullets lead with a compound noun stack ('backtested Java capacity-planning logic', 'legacy test-data workflow tool', 'topic-scoring research tool', 'EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check', 'RAG meal suggestions').
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Each stack forces a re-parse, and together they make the page read machine-compressed rather than spoken.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Unpack each stack into a verb phrase or a 'that' clause; keep one distinctive noun per bullet.

page_feedback.problem: Plain-language load is high in the middle of the page: 'Claude skill', 'sub-skills', 'LLM-as-judge', 'Bedrock classifier', 'AnyGrasp', 'Open3D', 'RAG', 'SentenceBERT' all appear within about 12 lines, and most aren't explained.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A non-specialist recruiter can't restate about four of the bullets, so the 'backend/systems' story gets diluted into 'lots of AI tools'.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: In each AI bullet, keep the one distinctive noun that explains the engineering. Put the rest into a plain description of what the system does.

page_feedback.problem: Nearly every bullet fills two full lines and several stack 3-5 product names (React Flow, Jest, EventBridge, Bedrock, Open3D, Prisma).
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The page looks dense; the eye lands on bold numbers but the surrounding sentences are tiring to read, which lowers human voice and plain language.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Move tool names that don't explain a decision to Technical Skills; the Skills section already lists most of them.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists tools with no supporting bullet: OpenSearch, SQLAlchemy, API Gateway, CloudWatch, PyTorch, Node.js, Jira, Agile, psutil. 'data structures and algorithms' as a skill is filler.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical reader treats unsupported entries as keyword padding and starts discounting the rest of the list.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut entries that you can't point to on the page or discuss in depth; drop 'data structures and algorithms' and 'Agile'.

page_feedback.problem: What a backend interviewer would dig into: (1) Redis category tree: cache key design, refresh and invalidation, and what the 'permission and rate limits' were; (2) S3 to Kinesis: where the 34% came from, and the batching, ordering and retry semantics in Lambda; (3) the 1 fill out of 99,123 that didn't match, and how it was debugged; (4) B+ tree vs LSM: the write-amplification tradeoff behind the '27% more disk'; (5) the Tortuga cache hit rate. Of these, (1) and (5) have the weakest written support.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These are the follow-ups the page invites. The candidate is well set up for (2) through (4). (1) and (5) currently end at intent, so the answer has to come entirely from the interview.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Clarify the constraint and key in the Capital One search-tool bullet. Say what was cached in the Tortuga bullet. No new metrics are needed.

page_feedback.problem: No bullet shows API design or service ownership (endpoints, request handling, schemas) even though 'REST APIs' and 'API Gateway' are listed under Skills.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: General backend postings ask for API and service experience by name. Here the claim exists only in Skills, so an interviewer may probe it without any bullet to anchor the answer.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: If any existing project (e.g. the Amazon Leo topic-scoring tool or Tortuga) exposed an API the candidate built, name it in that bullet's wording. Otherwise leave it in Skills only and don't invent it.

page_feedback.problem: Three concurrent college-year roles plus a co-founder role, with one bullet at UMIACS and one at AWS, spread thin evidence across many headers.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptic wonders how deep each commitment is. Thin single-bullet entries reinforce that doubt.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No new facts needed; make sure each single-bullet role's bullet states Amar's own deliverable clearly (see AWS and UMIACS bullet feedback).

page_feedback.problem: Bolding is inconsistent: 90%, 65%, 93%, 50.9M, 12.8x and 1.26M events/sec are bold, but 34% (Kinesis) and 99,122 of 99,123 are not.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The 99,122/99,123 fill-accuracy result, arguably the most convincing number on the page, gets less visual weight than a survey percentage.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Pick one rule (one bold per bullet on the headline result) and apply it consistently. Consider bolding the fill-match instead of 50.9M.
